title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E838 §§4–10 tries to correct the tabular longitude of the Moon's node and the orbital inclination using timed lunar eclipses. On this page Euler applies the 'safer' formula of §6, which uses only the beginning and end of the eclipse, to the partial eclipse of 1731 June 19. The mid-eclipse is 13h58'15" mean time.

(1) Tabular values. Euler takes the mean node longitude 9s8°45'38" and adds his table equations.
- Node-longitude equations: −1'12" (Moon's mean anomaly), −1'19" (Sun's mean anomaly), −31'52" (node−Sun elongation, the large Newtonian-type term), 0 (Sun−Moon), −2'23" (node−Moon). The total is −36'46", so the true node is 9s8°8'52".
- Inclination: 5°16'35" −42" +36" gives ρ = 5°16'29", so ½ρ = 2°38'15".
- With the shadow (anti-Sun) longitude 8s28°5'41", the shadow-centre distance from the node is x = −10°3'11".

(2) Physical data (§8). From the anomalies V (Sun) and v (Moon), with cosines reduced to the first quadrant, Euler derives:
- Sun's diameter 31'41" and parallax 12"; hourly motion m = 143".
- Moon's diameter 32'55" and parallax 59'38"; hourly motion n = 2195".
- Shadow semidiameter α = π_moon + π_sun − s_sun = 44'0" − ½" (no atmospheric enlargement), and β = 16'27½". Hence f = α + β = 60'27".
- Observed duration h = 14h40'41" − 13h14'21" = 1h26'20" = 1.4389 h.
- With nodal hourly motion k = 8": a = ½h(n+k) = 1585" = 26'25" (Moon's travel relative to the node in the half-duration) and b = ½h(m+k) = 109" = 1'49" (shadow's travel relative to the node).

(3) Small correction c (§9). Formula: c = (m+n+2k) sin2x tan²(½ρ)/[(n−m) sin1"]. With m+n+2k = 2354, n−m = 2052 and 2x = −20°6'22", this gives c = −2'53".

(4) Solving for x. The §6 relation is
[cos(a+b) + sin(a+b)tan(2x−c)] / [cos(a+b) − sin(a+b)tan(2x−c)] = R,
where R = [cos f − cos²(½ρ)cos(a−b+c)] / [cos f − cos²(½ρ)cos(a−b−c)].
Solving the linear-fractional equation gives tan(a+b)·tan(2x−c) = (R−1)/(R+1). Numerically (R−1):(R+1) = −120:39776, so −tan(2x−c) = 120/[39776 tan(28'14")]. Hence −(2x−c) = 20°10'14", 2x = −20°13'7" and x = −10°6'34". This is 3'23" more negative than the tables. On the next page Euler concludes the true node is 9s8°12'15", i.e. the tabular node should be advanced by about 3'23" (cf. 5'47" from the previous eclipse). He then extracts ρ and finally admits the determination is ill-conditioned: three unknowns (x, ρ, c) against two timing equations.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. I recomputed: the correction sums (−36'46"; 5°16'29"); x = −10°3'11"; the reduced cosines of V, v, 2v, v−V; α = 43'59.5"; h = 1.43889 h; a ≈ 1584.9"; b ≈ 108.6"; c ≈ 172.6" ≈ 2'53"; a±b and a−b±c.
The ratio 120:39776 checks to within rounding (I get about 120:39786). The final angle ≈ 20°10' agrees.

Methodological weakness, acknowledged by Euler on the next page: the numerator '120' is a difference of two nearly equal quantities (about 0.0019833 vs 0.0019953). It is known to only 2–3 significant figures, so an error of a few seconds in f, ρ or the timings shifts x by arcminutes.
c itself depends on the unknowns x and ρ, so the procedure is really a one-step fixed-point iteration seeded with tabular values. Treating c as known is a further gap, again acknowledged in §10.

ideas.what: Correcting the tabular node longitude from the observed start and end times of a lunar eclipse via spherical-trigonometric conditions of first and last contact
ideas.modern_name: Differential correction of orbital elements from eclipse contact timings
ideas.usually_credited_to: Long tradition (Ptolemy; Halley; Tobias Mayer and Lalande in the 18th century)
ideas.where_published: E838 (Opera postuma 1862); related eclipse methods in Euler's lunar works, but exact correspondence unsure

ideas.what: Table equations for node longitude and inclination as functions of the anomalies and the node–Sun and node–Moon elongations
ideas.modern_name: Periodic perturbations of the lunar node and inclination (main term in 2(☊−☉))
ideas.usually_credited_to: Newton (Principia III) and Machin; refined by Euler, Clairaut, Mayer
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar tables (Theoria motus lunae 1753, E187, and related tables)

ideas.what: Explicit recognition that the problem is ill-conditioned and underdetermined (3 unknowns, 2 equations), motivating the use of total eclipses with four contacts
ideas.modern_name: Observability / conditioning of a parameter-estimation problem
ideas.usually_credited_to: General 18th-century practice; formalized later (Gauss, least squares)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine, correct numerical application of eclipse-reduction formulas to correct Euler's own lunar tables. The only historically interesting datum, that his tabular node longitudes appear a few arcminutes too small, is minor and stated in the printed text.
transcription_corrections: Line '§ 9 ... atque 2x = —20°6'22"' is partly cut off at the right margin in the scan; the value 20°6'22" is consistent with x = −10°3'11".
'a — b — c = 27'29"' is partly cut at the margin but correct.
